title: Logs, metrics, traces and actionable alerts
objectives: Compute an explicit bounded terminal-outcome window with error denominators, unknown timeout latency, known-sample nearest-rank percentile and noncumulative histogram units.
Distinguish metrics/logs/traces and design actionable user-impact alerts with window, threshold, sample/no-data policy and diagnosis limits rather than equating a quiet rule with healthy service.
Apply logs, metrics, traces and actionable alerts invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: Metrics summarize numerical behavior across a declared population/window; structured logs record events; traces connect spans across a request path. None alone explains every failure.

blocks.md: Metrics summarize numerical behavior across a declared population/window; structured logs record events; traces connect spans across a request path. None alone explains every failure. Correlation IDs help link evidence but are not authentication or metric labels to attach unboundedly. OpenTelemetry describes broad baseline signals plus deeper system-specific diagnostics. Google SRE emphasizes useful latency/traffic/error/saturation signals and alerts tied to user experience. This example computes only terminal-observation error/latency summaries, not saturation, distributed traces or a live exporter.

Own rows are (observed_at_ms,known_duration_ms_or_None,outcome ok/error/timeout). Select terminal observation timestamps in [start,end), not request-start cohorts. Error ratio=(error+timeout)/all selected terminal observations. Timeout duration is UNKNOWN in this schema and cannot be inserted as zero. Known durations include ok AND error rows. A completed-only window can miss stuck requests until timeout events arrive; independent in-flight/deadline/black-box instrumentation is needed. Events may be late/missing/duplicated at ingestion; this pure array function does not authenticate or deduplicate them.

blocks.title: Error and latency denominators differ
items: At window [0,400), observe ok duration 10, error duration 100 and timeout duration unknown. A later terminal observation 1400 with duration 1000 is outside. Events 3, bad 2, error ratio 2/3.
Only 2 durations are known. Nearest-rank p95 uses ceil(.95*2) =2, so known-sample p95 =100 ms. It is NOT a 95th percentile for all requests because the timeout latency is censored/unknown.

Noncumulative bins <=10, (10,100], (100,1000], >1000 are (1,1,0,0). Minimum 5 events yields insufficient-data; minimum 3 and strict bad_ratio>0.1 yields alert. Empty window yields no-data, not zero-error health.

blocks.caption: Expected 3 2 2/3; 2 1 100; (1,1,0,0); insufficient-data; alert; no-data. Complete pure source, max 256 rows, integer milliseconds, strict enum/type/domain checks. Alert helper recomputes from validated raw events/window rather than trusting a caller-supplied summary. Own error-only threshold is not an SLO/error-budget monitoring deployment. No dashboard, network, pager or persistent store created.

blocks.md: Aggregate error counts and total counts before dividing; unweighted mean of per-shard error ratios can misweight small shards. Do not average p95 values and call it aggregate p95. Merge raw samples or compatible histogram bucket counts with their approximation/unknown-sample limits. Our bins are explicitly NONcumulative; some monitoring systems export cumulative buckets, so label semantics matter. Rate needs count divided by elapsed time with unit conversion; count alone is not requests per second.

An actionable alert names service/revision, SLI and eligible population, window, threshold, minimum-data/telemetry-loss policy, severity, owner, runbook, diagnostic links and recovery/reset conditions. Low traffic can make a single error dominate a ratio; Google SRE discusses precision/recall/detection/reset and low-traffic tradeoffs. A blanket minimum sample can hide a severe rare-request failure, so it is a teaching rule here, not a universal recommendation. within-error-threshold means only that this chosen rule did not fire, not proof of healthy latency/dependencies/security.

Metric labels should use bounded useful dimensions like operation/outcome rather than unique request/user/token IDs. High cardinality consumes storage/query resources and may expose private data. Put approved minimal correlation details in access-controlled logs/traces with retention/integrity policy; never log credentials or full payloads by default. Structured encoding helps prevent newline/log injection but does not make arbitrary sensitive content safe. Instrumentation overhead, dropped/sampled traces and delayed telemetry need visibility too.

Start with user impact and deployment/time scope, then inspect error classes, latency distribution, traffic and resource saturation, correlated dependency spans and safe logs. A correlated change is a lead, not root-cause proof. Distinguish error/timeout from business rejections and define denominator intentionally. A rule should not silently suppress the only evidence of a critical failure;test alert activation, reset, routing and missing-data behavior on the actual system. This source has no real on-call routing.

Independent transfer: enumerate window boundary and histogram boundary values, include all-timeout and empty windows, and reconstruct nearest rank with rational cumulative fractions. Merge two shards by counts and compare against combined raw events; construct a counterexample to averaging p95s. Propose a high-value low-traffic alert and explain why this minimum-count toy might miss it. Keep actual monitoring/backend/mobile visualization verification separate.

Sources: [Google SRE monitoring](https://sre.google/workbook/monitoring/), [SLO alerting/low traffic](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/), [OpenTelemetry broad/deep signals](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/how-to-write-conventions/t-shaped-signals/). Own terminal-window/nearest-rank/error rule is a bounded teaching contract, not these systems' implementation.

blocks.caption: Experiment: compose tail latency budgets across service stages.

guidedExercise.prompt: What should accompany a latency/error alert before it is actionable?
guidedExercise.solution: Service/revision, user-impact population, window/units/denominators, threshold/severity/minimum/no-data policy, owner/runbook and safe diagnostic links; test routing/reset/telemetry gaps. Unknown timeouts/censoring and sampling/cardinality/privacy limits remain. A pure summary/rule is not a deployed monitor or root-cause proof.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Logs, metrics, traces and actionable alerts" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: Missing duration and observed zero differ. (Keep the known-sample denominator visible.)
A quiet rule is limited evidence. (Latency/security/dependencies may still fail.)
Both error and timeout count as bad in this contract.
realWorldApplication: In practice, engineering teams apply logs, metrics, traces and actionable alerts within Production Integration and Capstone when building reliable production engineering and distributed systems workflows — specifically to compute an explicit bounded terminal-outcome window with error denominators, unknown timeout latency, known-sample nearest-rank percentile and noncumulative histogram units.
quantFinanceApplication: Desk workflows in Production Integration and Capstone rely on logs, metrics, traces and actionable alerts across production engineering, distributed systems, software engineering, keeping numerical estimates, risk bounds, and low-latency paths predictable.
summary: Declare population, window, units and every denominator.
Unknown timeout latency is not zero; known-sample percentiles do not describe missing samples.
No-data/insufficient-data and a quiet error-only rule are not service health.
Actionable alerts and safe bounded telemetry need actual operational tests.

quiz.prompt: Should unknown timeout latency enter this percentile as zero?
options: Yes, to keep every row numeric
quiz.explanation: Missing duration and observed zero differ. (Keep the known-sample denominator visible.)

options: This chosen error rule did not fire
quiz.explanation: A quiet rule is limited evidence. (Latency/security/dependencies may still fail.)

quiz.prompt: Three terminal events, two bad. What bad count?
quiz.explanation: Both error and timeout count as bad in this contract.

quiz.prompt: How should compatible shard error ratios be aggregated?
options: Sum bad and total counts, then divide
Use the smallest error count only
quiz.explanation: Reconcile denominator populations before combining. (This weights events rather than shards.)

quiz.prompt: Why can minimum event counts be risky for rare high-value requests?
options: They discard only statistically unimportant requests
They can suppress serious low-traffic failures
quiz.explanation: The toy rule is not a universal paging policy. (Alert policy must reflect user impact.)
